# Nandiyamigarājajātaka (Ja 385)
**ID:** Ja 385
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1

**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja385

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nandiyamigarājajātaka* (Ja 385, also known as the *Nandiyamigajātaka* or *Nandiya Jātaka*) is a canonical birth story situated at the beginning of the *Avāriyavagga* in the Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883; SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing narrative set at Jetavana, the Buddha related this story after discovering that a certain monk was supporting his lay parents; praising the monk for upholding the noble conduct of ancient sages who sacrificed their lives for their parents even when born as beasts, the Buddha recounted an episode from a previous life [SuttaCentral].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as Nandiya, a deer king (*migarājā*) possessed of elephant-like strength who attends to his elderly mother and father [Fausböll 1883; Readings from the Jatakas]. When Nandiya is threatened by a royal hunting party, his unwavering practice of loving-kindness (*mettā*) demonstrates transformative efficacy, rendering the hunter-king completely unable to release his lethal arrow [Shaw 2006]. The Jātaka is commonly cited in studies of Buddhist meditation as an illustration of the protective and almost magical power of *mettā* as one of the Bodhisatta's perfections (*pāramī*) [Shaw 2006]. The narrative concludes with the traditional identification of characters (*samodhāna*), identifying the king of the past as the disciple Ānanda and the deer king Nandiya as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].
Text-reuse calculations by DharmaNexus show ten shared segments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (specifically in volume 3, Atk S0513a3, with the longest match running from §4.1–6.4 to §2455–2462) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records cross-language matches across eight segments with the Tibetan translation of the *Mahopāyakauśalyabuddhapratyupakāra-sūtra* (D0353) [DharmaNexus].
